2.05 The Breaks of the Rio Grande, delineated by Trowbridge (1932), is a moderately to steeply rolling tributary area of the Rio Grande between the Balcones Escarpment and the Rio Grande delta. The "Breaks" varies from 1 to 15 miles in width and is bordered by plains which slope gently toward the Gulf. This essentially featureless upland surface is broken by the landward-facing Bordas Scrap near Rio Grande City. The Scarp, supported by the resistant Goliad formation, trends northward and averages about 70 feet in height.
2.06 Structure. Geologic structure upstream from Amistad Reservoir is relatively complex. The Solatario and Marathon uplifts in the Big Bend area have produced numerous major faults and block fault mountain chains. The area between El Paso and Big Bend is only slightly less disturbed, with predominantly northwestward trending mountain chains produced by the Van Horn uplift. The Edwards Plateau can be characterized as a level-topped upland representing a broad, slightly uplifted, mildly flexured and faulted peneplain. In the lower Rio Grande Valley the dominant structural feature is the Rio Grande Grande Embayment, a landward extension of coastal downwarping. The axis of the embayment coincides approximately with the river and is evident as far northward as the Lake Amistad area where it exists as a broad syncline with gently sloping limbs. Superimposed on this broad syncline, smaller anticlines and synclines alternate in parallel arrangement with the regional synclinal axis. The Balcones Escarpment is weakly defined in the Del Rio area and the Balcones zone of major faulting (Balcones Fault Zone) apparently does not extend west of the Uvalde area. Downstream from the Dam, Cretaceous, Tertiary, and Quarternary formations dip gently gulfward at rates which vary from 40 to 130 feet per mile.
2.07 Stratigraphy. Geologic formations in the lower Rio Grande basin range in age from lower Cretaceous to Recent, and with the exception of the Pliocene-Pleistocene gravels, they outcrop in successively younger bands in a gulfward direction. During late Pliocene or early Pleistocene times, continental deposition of sands and gravels occurred on the Gulf Coastal Plain. The Uvalde gravels are erosional remnants of these deposits now capping interstream divides and overlying strata of various ages between the Balcones Escarpment and the Bordas Scarp. Several Uvalde gravel terraces of large areal extent occur near the Rio Grande between Eagle Pass and Laredo.
2.08 Soils. Rio Grande alluvium is composed of lenses of gravel, sand, silt, and clay in various combinations. The gravel is well-rounded, and sizes up to 3 or 4 inches are common. The alluvial thickness ranges from twenty to about thirty feet between the dam and Eagle Pass. Granular materials predominate above Vega Verde Addition (approximately 5 miles below the dam). Grain sizes passing the 200 sieve (barely visible) made up only 3 to 10 percent by weight of samples taken in this reach, with the percentage of fine sizes increasing in a downstream direction. About 20 to 50 percent of the banks between the Dam and Eagle Pass are vertical or near vertical indicating active erosion and sloughing. Sloughing is caused both by erosion and by the discharge of bank storage water during low river stages. The sandy more permeable lenses in the channel banks are more susceptible to the latter sloughing action. Most vertical banks observed were 5 to 6 feet in height during moderate flows.
2.09 Ground Water. The Edwards and Associated Limestones is the principal ground water aquifer in Val Verde and Kinney Counties. This aquifer includes in descending order the Georgetown limestone, Kiamichi formation, Edwards limestone, and Comanche Peak limestone. These formations are connected hydrologically in most of northern Val Verde County. North of a line near the 29°45' latitude, the Kiamichi is absent or not recognized.
